description: We are Heartbeat, a team of university students passionate about space exploration and programming, participating in the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge.
summary: Heartbeat is a health self-assessment platform for astronauts on long-duration missions. Astronauts use an offline-first desktop app to log routine check-ups (blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep) as well as radiation doses, cabin environment and eye pressure. A shared rules engine compares every reading with sourced reference ranges and turns it into a traffic light for each of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, with plain-language guidance and an escalation message when something is critical. Because a deep-space crew cannot count on a live link, everything is evaluated on board and queued; when the link returns, an idempotent sync delivers it to a Mission Control web portal where flight surgeons review each astronaut, acknowledge alerts and reply, under role-based permissions. A Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 streams the astronaut's live heart rate to both apps, and daily Samsung Health data (sleep, activity, blood pressure) can be pulled in. Heartbeat gives crews a way to notice and act on changes in their own health, and gives the ground the same picture as soon as contact is restored.
details:
What it does

Heartbeat helps astronauts on long-duration missions notice changes in their own health and act on them, even with no link to Earth, and gives Mission Control the same picture as soon as contact returns.

Astronaut desktop app (offline-first). Each astronaut signs in to their own profile (sign-in also works offline) and records routine check-ups: blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours and mood, plus radiation doses, cabin environment and eye pressure/vision. Every reading is evaluated on board against sourced reference ranges and shown as normal, watch or critical (always with a text label, never color alone) with plain-language guidance. Critical results say who to contact and let the astronaut send a report to the ground.

Status at a glance. A traffic light for each of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environments) and an overall status, each with a short explanation, a 3-step onboarding and a small glossary (mSv, CO₂, SANS, PVT).

Mission Control web portal. Crew overview, astronaut detail with current status and history, a mission view (distance, communication delay, gravity, crew status by hazard), alerts that flight surgeons acknowledge, two-way messages, and administration with predefined roles plus a checklist of permissions.

Smartwatch. A Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 sends the astronaut's heart rate every second; it appears live in both apps through SignalR. Daily Samsung Health data (sleep, activity, historical heart rate, blood pressure) is pulled in through WatchSync, a companion service.

Optional AI assistant. Disabled by default, it uses Anthropic's Claude to explain in plain language the status and open alerts that Heartbeat has already calculated. It never takes part in evaluation and receives no credentials or personal notes.

How it works

One ASP.NET Core backend on .NET 10 exposes two APIs: a Crew API for the desktop app and a Mission Control API for the portal, secured with ASP.NET Core Identity, JWT and permission-based policies. The evaluation logic (reference ranges, the five-hazard rules engine, the radiation model, vision analysis and check-up streaks) lives in a shared library, Heartbeat.Shared, used by both the server and the desktop app, so an astronaut sees offline exactly the result the server computes later.

The desktop app stores everything in local SQLite with a store-and-forward queue. When the link with Earth is available, an idempotent sync pushes check-ups, doses, messages and profile edits and pulls replies, alert acknowledgements and updated ranges. Repeating a sync never duplicates data, and rejected items come back with a reason without blocking the rest.

Benefits and impact

It works where a web-only tool would fail, because it is offline-first by design. It turns raw numbers into one clear status per hazard, with guidance, for crew members who are not doctors. It gives flight surgeons a consistent view after communication gaps. The same approach applies on Earth to people in isolated, hazardous jobs (mining, Antarctic stations, submarines, offshore platforms); the catalog already includes those profiles with their own thresholds.

Tools and technologies

C# and .NET 10; ASP.NET Core minimal APIs; Entity Framework Core with SQLite; ASP.NET Core Identity and JWT; SignalR; WPF with CommunityToolkit.Mvvm (desktop); Blazor Web App (portal); xUnit, including an automated end-to-end scenario (solar particle event, high CO₂ and sleep deprivation recorded offline, then synced); GitHub Projects and GitHub Actions; Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 and Samsung Health; WatchSync (Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL); Anthropic Claude API for the optional assistant.

What makes it creative

The same rules engine runs on board and on the ground, so offline and online results always match. Health is organized around NASA's five hazards rather than a flat list of vitals. A live wearable stream sits alongside an offline-first check-up routine. And every threshold says where it comes from and how confident we are in it.

Factors we considered

Intermittent communication and delay; crew members without medical training; privacy (each astronaut sees only their own data, and Mission Control access depends on permissions); accessibility and safety: Heartbeat is a decision-support and self-assessment tool, not a medical device, and it does not diagnose.
